title: Sandbox Experiments
summary: Sandbox Experiments identifies and explores the critical design, workflow and organisational questions that determine system success or failure before Creative Navy commits to a product frame or detailed system design.

bodySections.heading: Sandbox Experiments in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Sandbox Experiments is the initial exploration phase in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. The phase identifies and explores the critical challenges that will determine whether a platform succeeds or fails under real constraints. These are not features to build. They are fundamental questions the platform must answer.

Creative Navy typically begins Sandbox Experiments by identifying 4–8 key platform challenges. These are the points where design decisions have the highest impact, such as how multi-role workflows should coordinate without bottlenecks, how complex data can remain readable under time pressure, or how the system should behave when constraints conflict.

bodySections.heading: Sandbox Experiments Treats Design as Research
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments uses design-as-research in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method: Creative Navy learns by building, observing how possible solutions perform against real constraints, and understanding the terrain through making. The phase is not concept generation followed by research. Discovery and invention happen together.

In Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, software is treated as something that changes the reality it represents. If design work only follows a list of what users or stakeholders already stated, it stays inside the existing paradigm. Sandbox Experiments instead maps what is and what could be. Prototypes, observations, competitive benchmarks, technical constraints and stakeholder reactions interrogate one another.

Sandbox Experiments can produce information that conventional requirements gathering does not produce. A prototype can make an implicit requirement visible by forcing a stakeholder to react to a specific alternative workflow. A field observation can reveal physical context that would be missed by structured measurement. A speculative prototype can make a future value proposition concrete enough for stakeholders to assess.

bodySections.heading: Option Space Mapping Explores Alternatives Before Convergence
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Option space mapping is central to Sandbox Experiments when the problem can be explored through design alternatives. Creative Navy systematically explores 3–6 variants per challenge before converging. Each experiment produces evidence about what works in context, what fails, which assumptions do not hold, and which problems are genuinely hard.

The output is not a single preferred concept. Sandbox Experiments produces a library of tested approaches for each key challenge, evidence about working and failing directions, and a clearer understanding of the terrain. This protects against early commitment to a weak product frame and reduces the risk of expensive pivots when initial assumptions fail under real use.

KISPE Space shows option space mapping with a documented counting convention. KISPE Space is a UK space systems engineering company, and the product was a common space operating picture. The engagement defined and explored 12 UX challenges across product organisation, map control, area selection, time, satellite services, imagery, alerts, information quality, field versus desktop, limited connectivity, sharing, and technical transparency. Creative Navy recorded 36 concept alternatives across those 12 challenges, represented in 64 low-fidelity frames. The deliverable documented the counting convention: one frame meant one distinct conceptual screen or interaction state; colour and spacing variants were not counted separately; a revision or re-annotation of an existing frame was not a new frame. The exploration did not include user research of any kind.

Raymarine shows option space mapping inside a constrained product architecture problem. The exploration work used two delivery sprints, which were not method phases. The first sprint ran for five working days and covered product and engineering alignment, mapping of core communication tasks and error paths, comparison of product architectures, wireframing of AIS list, plot and hybrid screens, and scenario walkthroughs. Nine exploration challenges were recorded, each with three named alternatives, a recorded direction, a decision basis and a named downstream consequence. Physical controls were added as a tenth challenge during the work. No competing product was evaluated, and the exploration was bench-and-document work with no field research, no sea trials and no on-vessel work.

Schone Airspace Group shows option space mapping combined with hands-on operation as domain learning. The product is referred to descriptively as mission control. Creative Navy defined and explored 15 design challenges across core architecture, priority planning, high-consequence operation, and supporting operations. Creative Navy recorded 45 concept alternatives across those 15 challenges, represented in 85 low-fidelity frames. The deliverable documented the counting convention: one frame meant one distinct screen structure or meaningful operating state; label and spacing revisions were not counted separately; shared instruments, maps and panels were reused rather than redrawn as independent designs. Creative Navy had hands-on access to the live product and drove the running system during the engagement. That access was domain learning, not an audit. User research entered late, at the end of UX development, as validation and correction; the exploration ran on task analysis, published human factors material, hands-on operation of the running product and structured expert analysis.

bodySections.heading: Sandbox Instruments Are Chosen to Fit the Terrain
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments does not require one fixed research protocol in Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy chooses the instrument according to the terrain: unstructured situated observation for a failing system with no useful baseline, prototype-driven interrogation for an ossified organisation, prototype-driven value elicitation for a system that does not yet exist, or feasibility exploration when the first question is whether the problem is solvable by design.

In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device work, Creative Navy used deliberate unstructured observation of a failing patient interface. Creative Navy travelled to the client in France and conducted four observation sessions of the existing patient interface in use. The decision not to measure was deliberate. A prior internal test by the client had produced 2 completions from 14 users, a completion rate so low that structured measurement would add little design information. The field visits produced situated understanding of the physical relationship between patient and screen, how confusion appeared in body movement before abandonment, the scan sequence and its physical demands, and the absence of guidance when a step was unclear. That observation became the evidence base for the Inform–Prevent–Correct framework introduced in Concept Convergence.

In the UNICEF internal planning, approval and reporting tool, Creative Navy used prototypes as an organisational diagnostic instrument. UNICEF arrived with an ossified status quo and no clear requirements. The central organisation's initial framing attributed low-quality submissions to local-office reluctance and an inconvenient interface, while research across four intensively engaged local offices revealed a cross-tier comprehension gap. Over a 3-month Sandbox Experiments phase, Creative Navy produced 26 prototypes reviewed by 56 stakeholders across two organisational tiers. The prototypes forced stakeholders to explain why reporting worked as it did. In several cases, long-standing mandatory requirements could not be convincingly justified and were removed, consolidated or substantially simplified. A downstream client-measured outcome recorded a 45% reduction in compliance issues nine months post-rollout; the documented account traces that outcome to the Sandbox work that resolved the mental-model mismatch and rationalised requirements before production screens were built.

In the Neugo UK visa application case-management platform, Creative Navy used Sandbox Experiments as value elicitation for a system that did not yet exist. The 7-week engagement was not a build. Its purpose was to produce a prototype for a process to lobby the government to commission the system and to give backers something concrete enough to commit to. Creative Navy worked with the Home Office and four legal firms in value-elicitation mode, using concrete possibilities to provoke value recognition while keeping those possibilities tied to stakeholder operating conditions. The output was a value/desirability mapping and a clickable Figma prototype. Client-reported evidence says the engagement contributed to the system being commissioned, that stakeholders attributed roughly 30% of the decision factors to the design, and that dedicated demo sessions were built around the prototype.

In the handheld C2 engagement, the client was a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them. The scope covered interface structure, task behaviour, information priority and the clarity of operator control. It did not extend to autonomy, control algorithms, autonomous safety behaviour, the datalink, the effector, targeting logic, or any certification or weapons-review activity. The delivery plan set the first test of the swarm designs as whether the problem was solvable by design at all, before any comparison of design merits, because the client was not certain it was. It was solvable, and the swarm capability was built. This is Sandbox exploration with a stop condition. Creative Navy has no primary field evidence on this engagement: no contextual observation, no field visits and no interviews.

bodySections.heading: Sandbox Experiments Can Redefine the Client's Initial Problem
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments is designed to test whether the initial product frame is the right frame. The maritime VTS engagement shows Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method producing a different problem definition from the one the client brought.

The client was a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations and waterway operators. The work identified 31 candidate interaction patterns, classified into three groups: 18 potentially common patterns, 8 conditional patterns requiring product-specific contracts, and 5 patterns that had to remain permanently separate. The patterns that had to remain separate were radio transmit and physical push-to-talk, lock gate actuation, navigation alert authority, standards-bound chart portrayal, and shipboard terminal controls.

The recommendation replaced the client's starting ambition of a common modern interface across nine products with a different structure: one application developed to full depth as a reference, a technology-neutral semantic design system built in parallel, bounded transfer tests in four other products, and implementation contracts and governance handed to the client's engineers. The reason was that a cosmetic refresh could make a mixed alert region visually quieter while preserving interpretation risk, and a broadly reusable status component could conceal whether a radio resource was unselected, unavailable or configured for transmission.

Field observation in this engagement happened in operational VTS control rooms at a customer site with the client's end customers' operators, using sanitised scenarios rather than live traffic. This evidence boundary matters: the engagement included control-room observation, but the observations do not transfer to adjacent engagements such as Raymarine or KISPE Space.

bodySections.heading: Triangulation in Sandbox Experiments Looks for Discrepancies, Not Confirmation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy uses triangulation in Sandbox Experiments as detective work. Each research method is used against the others to find discrepancies and hidden nuance, not only to confirm common patterns.

A stakeholder account may identify feature X as important because it saves time. User evidence may identify feature X as important because mistakes take a long time to resolve. These look similar at the surface, but they point to different design work. The underlying problem may be error resolution time, not the feature itself. That nuance can then be tested against stakeholder reasoning, competitor handling of error prevention, and technical constraints.

The UNICEF engagement shows the same form of triangulation at organisational level. The central organisation's stated problem was a cumbersome interface. Research indicated that local offices did not understand why the system existed or how their input was used. Those are different design problems. The first points toward usability improvement; the second points toward meaning-making and cross-tier communication. Prototypes made the difference legible to the organisation.

bodySections.heading: High-Value Sandbox Research Activities Expose Context and Capability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments can include user observation, having users teach Creative Navy how to use a system, or having team members attempt to do the user's job. The documented purpose is to expose silent patterns, conscious mental models, how users believe the system should work, how challenges change with experience, and what users would or would not be capable of if the system changed.

Context of use is treated as part of the design terrain. A tool is embedded in its operating context, and value often appears where the tool can be better integrated with that context. Users may also be more open with a third party than with their own provider. In the UNICEF engagement, local offices were more candid with Creative Navy about experiencing central requirements as performative bureaucracy than they had been within internal reporting lines.

Sandbox Experiments may also use a hunter rather than bureaucrat posture toward standard deliverables. The same deliverables, such as stakeholder interviews, user research and competitive analysis, produce different results depending on whether the team pursues the most informative participants, returns to a user after reflection, asks a difficult question, gains access to non-public software for benchmarking, or asks developers to reconsider constraints because a changed perspective may create value.

bodySections.heading: Architecture Work Starts Inside Sandbox Experiments
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy begins architecture deliverables inside Sandbox Experiments. Iteration 1 is a logic-first baseline. Iteration 2 explores opinionated extremes. Later architecture iterations are treated in the Iterative System Building material.

This placement matters because Sandbox Experiments is not only research intake. The phase begins shaping system logic while uncertainty is still visible. It uses design artefacts to test and expose the questions that later phases must resolve.

bodySections.heading: Outputs of Sandbox Experiments
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments produces a library of tested approaches for each key challenge. It records evidence about what works and fails, identifies assumptions that do not hold, and distinguishes genuinely hard problems from problems that only appeared hard.

Sandbox Experiments can also produce option-space maps, low-fidelity frames, prototype libraries, value/desirability maps, benchmark findings, task walkthroughs, expert critiques, feasibility gates, and early architecture iterations. The exact output depends on the terrain of the engagement.

Durations vary. Focused problems can run for 2–3 weeks. Complex platforms can run for 2–3 months. Larger intergovernmental engagements can run longer. The UNICEF Sandbox Experiments phase ran for 3 months across two organisational tiers. A focused Sandbox-only engagement can also be shorter in scope: Neugo ran for 7 weeks and produced a fundable vision rather than proceeding immediately to full system design.

bodySections.heading: Boundaries and Evidence Limits in Sandbox Experiments
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Sandbox Experiments is not always structured user research. KISPE Space had no user research of any kind. Raymarine had no field research, no sea trials and no on-vessel work. Schone Airspace Group used user research late, at the end of UX development, as validation and correction rather than research-led discovery. The handheld C2 engagement had no contextual observation, no field visits and no interviews.

Counting conventions do not migrate across engagements. KISPE Space, Schone Airspace Group, Raymarine and the maritime VTS engagement count different things under different conventions. Their figures should not be merged, averaged or compared as like-for-like measures.

Sandbox Experiments is not a certification, validation or safety assurance activity. In the handheld C2 engagement, Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; it did not design the system. In Schone Airspace Group, hands-on access to the running product was domain learning, not an audit. In the maritime VTS engagement, the work should not be read as a nine-product redesign or as a safety, certification or regulatory credential.
